headline: NAB's credit impairment charge (cash basis) rose $105 million or 14.4% to $833 million in FY25 from $728 million in FY24 — the bank's own stated movement — lifting the annualised charge to GLAs by 1bp to 0.11% (denominator: gross loans and acceptances). The results book's asset-quality note decomposes it: the individually assessed charge rose $328 million or 51.6% to $964 million (new and increased provisions 1,192 vs 863), partially offset by a $223 million swing in collective provisioning from a $92 million charge to a $131 million write-back. Where it arose: CIB +153 (charge of 146 vs net write-back of 7); New Zealand −104 (25 vs 129); Corporate Functions write-back −83 (122 vs 205); Personal Banking −33 (255 vs 288); B&PB +6 (529 vs 523) — the divisional deltas sum exactly to +105. On the statutory income statement the charge was 833 vs 741 (Δ+92); the $13m FY24 cash-vs-statutory gap is not itemised in the pages read, and FY25's only statutory adjustments (Note 15) do not touch impairment. The presentation corroborates: FY25 bar $833m, the largest since 2020, ratio 0.11% of GLAs.

limitations: Plan item 'cash earnings statement P&L line': the CIC line's FY25/FY24 columns are evidenced from the results book's asset-quality note table (PDF p26, ev-4) and Note 4 Provision for credit impairment (PDF p53, ev-41), which print the same line; the consolidated cash earnings statement page itself was not separately cited.

No waterfall chart of the FY25-v-FY24 CIC movement exists in the corpus; the quantified bridge is built from the results book's provision-type table (PDF p26) and the where-layer from the divisional tables, not from a walk chart.

The presentation's Group CIC chart (p26) is drawn on half-year bars (2H24 365 → 2H25 485): a context comparison. Its split of the collective line into 'underlying CP charge/(write-back)' and 'forward looking provisions' is published for half-years only (2H25: 0 and −89); no full-year split of the −223 is published, so FY collective sub-drivers are carried unquantified from the results-book prose.

New Zealand's AUD delta (−104, from 129 to 25) is computed from printed levels; the bank states the divisional movement in NZD (−NZ$114m, −80.9%; ex-FX −80.6%). NZD half-year bars on the presentation (129 = 27+102) corroborate the AUD total.
The $13m gap between the FY24 cash-basis CIC ($728m) and the statutory charge to the income statement ($741m) is not itemised in the pages read (FY25 has no such gap: both print 833).

The results book does not allocate each division's movement between individually assessed and collective components; the where-to-what mapping (e.g. BPB +6 combining higher home-lending individually assessed charges with lower collective business-lending charge) rests on the divisions' own narratives.
BPB and PB FY24 comparatives were restated for customer portfolio transfers between the divisions; the movement analysis uses the restated comparators.
Provision-balance movements (collective −163 to 5,002 incl. a $283m FLP release; individually assessed +407 to 1,163) are quoted as balance-sheet context and are not part of the charge bridge.
Cash and statutory movements do not differ in FY25 (both +105; the endpoints differ only in the FY24 base, 728 cash vs 741 statutory); no separate statutory driver table is shown.

Credit impairment charge increased by $105 million or 14.4% to $833 million, driven by a higher level of individually assessed credit impairment charge primarily in Corporate and Institutional Banking.
Individually assessed credit impairment charge increased by $328 million or 51.6% to $964 million mainly due to:

an increased charge in Corporate and Institutional Banking for the impairment of a small number of customers combined with the non-recurrence of write-backs and recoveries for a small number of customers in the September 2024 full year
a modest increase in charge across the Business and Private Banking and New Zealand Banking business lending portfolios and the unsecured retail portfolio in Personal Banking.
Collective credit impairment charge decreased by $223 million from a charge of $92 million to a write-back of $131 million.

The write-back for the September 2025 full year of $131 million was driven by a net release of forward-looking provisions, combined with the release of provisions held for customers that transferred to individually assessed during the September 2025 full year.

This was partially offset by the impact of volume growth in the Business and Private Banking business lending portfolio, combined with deterioration in asset quality across the Australian lending portfolio.

The charge for the September 2024 full year of $92 million was driven by deterioration in asset quality across the Group's lending portfolio combined with volume growth in Business and Private Banking.

This was partially offset by the impact of house price increases, the impact of model changes on provisions for the Group's underlying lending portfolio and a net release of forward-looking provisions.
